STAT 494: STATISTICAL GENETICS
A COMPARATIVE STUDY ON THE PREDICTIVE
POWERS OF LASSO, KNN AND SVM IN THE TASK
OF TUMOR CLASSIFICATION
Authors: Sam Price, and Tam NguyenNoah Shannon
Introduction, Motivation, and Data
Rationale
In the rapidly evolving field of computational biology, selecting appropriate analytical
methods is crucial for deriving meaningful insights from increasingly complex datasets.
Throughout our journal club sessions this semester, we have systematically reviewed
cutting-edge research applying machine learning approaches to biological data analysis.
These discussions revealed notable patterns in methodological choices that warrant
further exploration and synthesis.
Our class has traditionally focused on single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) data,
analyzing genetic variations at the most granular level to understand their associations with
phenotypic traits and disease susceptibility. SNP-level analyses have proven valuable for
identifying specific genetic markers and have been foundational to genome-wide
association studies (GWAS). However, they often present significant computational
challenges, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional data that includes millions of
variants across thousands of samples.
In contrast, the paper we reviewed for this project adopted a gene-centric analytical
approach, effectively "zooming out" from individual nucleotides to examine variation and
expression at the gene level. This shift in granularity, while sacrificing some fine-detail
resolution, offers several compelling advantages. Gene-level analyses can potentially
reduce dimensionality, mitigate multiple testing burdens, improve interpretability through
direct biological context, and enhance statistical power by aggregating signals across
multiple variants.
Data Context
The data we use for this project provides information on 12534 genes (number of columns)
belonging to 174 observations (number of rows). Below is a snippet of what it looks like.
2
The columns that start with capital letter D represent the genes and the `Class` column
consists of 11 tumor types we would like to identify. The values under any of the D columns
indicate how `on` a gene is during protein production. In other words, the larger the value,
the more actively that gene participates in such process.
Background Information
Machine Learning
Defined most broadly, machine learning is a field concerned with the development and
application of statistical algorithms that can learn from seen and then generalize onto
unseen data, performing tasks and quantifying relationships without explicit instructions.
Machine learning is widely used across almost every industry in the world as a robust tool
for prediction across regression and classification tasks. Rather than simply fitting a
regression like we might in a class like Stat 155, a machine learning approach has us split
the data into ‘train’ and ‘test’ sets. We use the training set to calibrate and ‘tune’ our model,
then at the very end use the unseen set aside test data as the true measure of
performance, simulating the application of the model in the real world.
3
One of the most common challenges faced in machine learning is the ‘curse of
dimensionality’, which arises when the efficiency and effectiveness of an algorithm or
model deteriorates as the dimensionality of the data increases, leading to overfitting,
spurious correlations, and computational complexity. This will be a recurring problem our
models seek to address in this project.
Overfitting is an abstract but critical term to understand when building or interpreting
machine learning models, and it applies to both regression and classification prediction
tasks. The ‘fit’ of a model, or how the model understands the relationship or shape present
in the data, can be roughly categorized in three ways:
1. Underfit: A model is underfit when it is too simple to capture the true relationship
in the data. As we see in both of the visual examples below, an underfit model might
ascribe a linear relationship to two variables, when the relationship is more
complex. Since the model is failing to capture the true complexity of the
relationship, it is underfit.
2. Overfit: The opposite of underfit, but also bad! A model is overfit when it mistakes
random noise or idiosyncrasies in the training data for generalizable aspects of the
true relationship between the variables. The model clings too closely to the training
data, creating a force or too good to be true fit that fails to generalize to new data
with different random noise.
3. Well-Fit. The goal. A well fit model strikes the balance between under and
overfitting, capturing the true relationship present in the data while not mistaking
random noise for true trends. While a well-fit model won’t be initially perfect on the
training set like an overfit model, it will perform better on unseen data (which is
where performance matters).
4
However, what happens when we can’t visually verify the fit of our model like we can in the
2-d figures? In the context of our project (and many others) high dimensional data and
models make such easy and intuitive observation difficult. Instead, we’ll use comparisons
between the training and test performance as our metric to avoid overfitting. If our test
accuracy is meaningfully lower than our training accuracy, it’s good evidence that our
model is over-adjusting to the training data at the cost of generalizability.
5
Models
LASSO
LASSO is a machine learning algorithm that stands for Least Absolute Shrinkage and
Selection Operator. It is an ordinary least squares regression with a penalty term called
lambda. The goal is to minimize the entire function.
This works by shrinking the coefficients, beta, down towards zero when they don’t
add much to the regression. This is useful in the context of genetic data because most large
genetic datasets have more columns than observations, so ordinary least squares cannot
be run. If coefficients are shrunk to zero that effectively eliminates columns in the data so
we are left with more observations than variables. In the coming paragraphs we will walk
through how to run LASSO in r and what some of the lines mean, using our data. This can
be followed along using the qmd file in the same folder as this README. This framework
can be applied to any form of data, not just the data we used. We use the test and training
splits that were used earlier, so that our metrics are being compared accurately.
6
We pull that data in and make all genes numeric and the Class variable a factor for
both the test and training data. Then we split the data into five folds for cross validation.
After that we define the model specification for the multinomial LASSO regression.
This code chunk works by using the multinom_reg() function from the parsnip package,
with penalty = tune() indicating that the regularization strength will be tuned later during
model selection. The mixture = 1 parameter sets the regularization to be pure LASSO,
rather than Ridge Regression or a mix of both. The model is then assigned the glmnet
engine, which fits regularized generalized linear models. Lastly, set_mode("classification")
tells parsnip that this is a classification model.
The lasso rec creates a preprocessing recipe for the modeling workflow. The formula
Class ~ . specifies that the outcome variable is Class, and all other variables in the dataset
tumor_train will be used as predictors. Then it standardizes all numeric predictor variables
by centering them to have a mean of zero and scaling them to have a standard deviation of
one. This normalization is important for models like LASSO, which are sensitive to the scale
of the input features. The resulting lasso_rec object defines how the data should be
preprocessed before being passed to the model during training and evaluation. Then the
workflow combines the recipe and model so that the data is always prepared the same way
before being used by the model.
7
We create a grid of ten lambda values to test how different levels of regularization
affect the model’s performance. After that we perform hyperparameter tuning by testing
different values of the regularization parameter (lambda) to find the best-performing
version of my LASSO model.
tune_grid(...): Tries out a bunch of different lambda values from penalty_grid, one by
one, to see which one helps the model perform best. It does that using the workflow
previously defined and the metrics line says what metrics to look at, while the control line
saves the results. We then graph these results and put them in a table. The next important
line of code is selecting the best lambda, which is done with the select by one standard
error function, which chooses the best lambda based on accuracy. It does this by using the
tune output data that was previously created, putting them in descending order of
accuracy, and picking the best lambda within one standard deviation of the actual best
lambda. We also ran this for sensitivity and found that the penalty term was the same, but
this may not be the case if this were to be run on other data. Below is a graph of how each
metric changes as lambda increases. As lambda increases all three metrics stay the same
and once lambda gets large enough they start to drop off. Showing how as too many
coefficients get shrunk to zero, the model loses accuracy.
8
Next we fit the data using finalize workflow, which makes sure to use the best
lambda on the workflow previously created then fits the data to all of the training data. We
then make predictions on the test data set. The code bind_cols places each prediction
alongside the actual class label and all the original features from the test dataset. We also
do this for the best lambda by sensitivity as a sanity check, to make sure the numbers are
the same.
We then take the final fit data and filter out all the coefficients that were not shrunk
down to zero and do the same form the sensitivity code. In this case we were left with 111
predictors, cut down from the thousands that were previously in the data. We then make a
confusion matrix showing how accurate our predictions were. The rest of the code is
outputting the metrics into a data table.
KNN
K-nearest neighbors, or KNN for short, is a classic but powerful machine learning algorithm
that classifies a data point on the basis of its k nearest neighbors. After a query point is
selected, a majority vote of the nearest neighbors is used to assign the new point to the
data class which has the most representatives within the nearest neighbors of the point.
9
KNN is a powerful algorithm because it is non-parametric, in other words it doesn’t make
assumptions about the underlying data. While a linear regression model inherently
assumes a linear relationship, a model like KNN doesn’t, allowing it to capture nuanced
classification and decision boundaries of complex relationships. KNN is also powerful
because of its simplicity, including only a few hyperparameters, or adjustable elements of
the model that can be used to refine performance. While ‘k’, or the number of neighbors
polled to classify a new point, is the main hyperparameter, one can also experiment with
the type of distance calculation used to define the ‘nearest’ neighbors in the first place (we
use classic Euclidean distance).
The behavior of the model changes as we adjust the number of nearest neighbors we take
into account, demonstrated by the figure above. If we only use 3 neighbors, we’ll classify
the query point as a triangle. However, if we use 7, we’ll classify it as a star. In general, the
fewer neighbors we use, the more volatile and dynamic our model becomes (adjectives
with positive connotation, but not inherently best in this context!), increasing the variance
but decreasing the bias. As we use more neighbors, the model becomes slower to adjust,
decreasing variance but increasing bias.
10
Shown by the plot below, after testing the performance of a variety of k values, using a
single nearest neighbor yielded the best accuracy for our KNN model.
This model used two strategies to address the curse of dimensionality, or p > n problem,
eventually yielding two distinct KNN models. The first was aggressive feature selection,
narrowing down the genes to only the most 100 predictors. The second was the use of
Principal Component Analysis, or PCA, as a feature selection tool. PCA attempts to reduce
the dimensionality of the data while preserving as much information as possible by
decomposing the predictor variables into linearly independent or orthogonal principal
components that are then used by the model as predictors. We’ll see how these strategies
panned out in the results section.
11
We took a couple of other standard machine learning steps when fitting this model, using
10-fold cross validation and normalizing feature scales to ensure no single gene dominated
on the basis of a large numerical range, which ensured the validity of our distance
measure.
SVM
How it works
The core of support vector machines lie in their power to increase the dimensional space
our data currently lives in. To illustrate why this is important, here is a little brain teaser
activity. Given a set of data points, can we find a line that separates the blue circles from
the red ones?
12
In this particular case, it is rather straightforward to pick as line that groups those circles by
the color, as is shown below:
However, real life data tends to be more complicated than the example provided above. In
fact, let’s consider this next case:
13
In this scenario, the answer might not be as obvious. As one soon may find out, there does
not exist a line such that the red and the blue circles are clearly separated. To solve this
problem, one useful trick is to change how the data points are represented by increasing
their current dimensional space. Specifically, one can choose to square the values of the
circles on the x axis (now a 1-dimensional space), effectively converting them to data
belonging to a new 2-dimensional space.
After the transformation, the task of finding the best decision boundary becomes slightly
easier than before. For this very simplified example, such dividing line can be constructed
as below
14
In actuality however, the algorithm does not physically change the data. It only does so
“abstractly” purely for the purpose of finding the best boundary. Our data therefore
remains intact.
Kernel
The conversion we demonstrated above can be dictated by a hyperparameter required for
SVM models, called the “kernel”. Some of the most commonly used ones include linear,
polynomial and radial. The process of squaring data in the previous example is done
through the “polynomial” kernel. As for the radial kernel , it is particularly useful in dealing
with highly non-linear data and to understand how it works is no easy task, Radial type is a
special, more complex case of transformation where data is augmented to some infinite
dimensional space, so intricate that there is no way to visually illustrate it.
It is also worth mentioning that as we play with these types of kernels and compare how
the model performs accordingly, we may derive some useful insights from the linearity of
the data we are using. For example, after running 3 aforementioned kernel types on the
tumors dataset, we learned that accuracy decreased the more complex we adjusted our
model to be
15
We can see from the image above that the linear version outperformed the other two, with
the radial classifier underperforming relative to the no-information rate, meaning it
performs worse than guessing the most frequent class.
So what can we say about the data? It is linear enough that we only need a linear
transformation to complete the classification task successfully, without the need to use
more complicated kernels, which may end up exacerbating the results.

Results/Conclusions
Overall Accuracy
After training all models and comparing the predictions against the test set, the accuracy
results can be interpreted as follows:
SVM achieved the highest overall accuracy, with LASSO and KNN performing comparably
well, whereas KNN with PCA lagged considerably behind the other models.
The results for KNN and KNN with PCA contradicted our expectations that incorporating
PCA would improve KNN’s performance. However, the opposite occurred, likely due to the
nature of PCA. PCA reduces dimensionality by selecting components that maximize
variance, without regard to class label relevance. As a result, it may have discarded features
that were important for distinguishing between classes, leading to an underfitting model.
This distortion of the feature space made distance-based comparisons—crucial for
KNN—less effective. In contrast, feature selection via Random Forest preserved
17
class-relevant information, enabling KNN to better capture the structure necessary for
accurate classification.
Accuracy by Class
The second results metric we used was model accuracy by class. The conclusions are
interesting. In general, every model struggles on Class 4. The KNN models struggle in
different ways, with the best features model uniquely struggling on Classes 1 and 8, and
PCA doing worse on class 2. SVM seems like the best overall, maintaining a high accuracy
percentage across all classes. Even when it does poorly, like on Class 4, it’s no worse than
the other models. LASSO is on average more consistent than KNN, but is the worst on Class
4.
Accuracy by class is important because it gives us a more granular understanding of the
overall accuracy score, and means that if we were to use a team or ensemble of models to
make a prediction, we could use accuracy by class as a tiebreaker if two models disagreed,
but one had superior accuracy in a given class area. However, it’s important to keep in mind
the limitations of this type of plot when working with such a small dataset. Using an 80/20
train/test split, our models were only exposed to 33 test data points, or just over 3
prediction attempts per class. Unfortunately, this makes it difficult to say for certain how
our models would do on a given class absent more observations to establish a more robust
trend.
18
Sensitivity/Specificity
The final metrics we used were sensitivity and specificity. Sensitivity is the true positive rate
and specificity is the true negative rate. When predicting a certain class, if we were to
predict not that class our specificity would still be very high, which is why we care the most
about sensitivity. We want to find, of the actual positives, how many did we actually predict
to be positive. We find that KNN and LASSO have nearly identical sensitivities and SVM is
close behind. KNN with PCA is lower but still has a high enough sensitivity to use if
necessary. We wouldn’t recommend using a single metric rather a combination of these,
with the first two choices being KNN and LASSO.
19
Main Conclusion
The three models—SVM, LASSO, and KNN (without PCA)—achieved similarly high overall
accuracies. Among them, SVM demonstrated the best performance in terms of both overall
and per-class accuracy. While KNN and LASSO occasionally outperformed SVM in metrics
such as sensitivity and specificity, the differences were minimal, typically within a margin of
0.01 to 0.02.
